literary_identity: Poet and novelist; the author of The Middle Parts of Fortune, the finest novel of the ordinary soldier in the First World War.
biography: Born Frederic Norton Manning in Sydney on 22 July 1882; he came to England with his family, worked in a solicitor's office and lived by his pen, publishing The Vigil of Brunhild (1907), Scenes and Portraits (1909) and Eidola (1917). He served in the Shropshire Light Infantry on the Somme and wrote The Middle Parts of Fortune (1929, published as Her Privates We in 1930). He died in London on 22 February 1935.
literary_profile: Frederic Manning wrote The Middle Parts of Fortune, the finest novel of the ordinary soldier in the First World War: its anonymity, its dialect and its unsparing record of the ranks made it the war's most complete fictional document, and it was admired by Hemingway, T. E. Lawrence and every later writer on the war.
stylistic_characteristics: The third-person narrative that stays with the ranks; the dialect speech of the soldiers; the unsparing detail of mud, hunger and fear; the absence of plot and rhetoric; the documentary exactness of the battalion.
intellectual_concerns: The First World War and the myth of sacrifice; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; shell shock, mourning, and the unquiet dead; mass society, the crowd, and the individual talent.
historical_significance: Frederic Manning wrote The Middle Parts of Fortune, the finest novel of the ordinary soldier in the First World War: its anonymity, its dialect and its unsparing record of the ranks made it the war's most complete fictional document, admired by Hemingway and Lawrence alike.

literary_identity: Poet, critic and anarchist; one of the Imagist poets of the First World War and the finest English art critic of his generation.
biography: Born Herbert Edward Read at Kirbymoorside, Yorkshire, on 4 December 1893; he served as a captain in the Green Howards on the Western Front, and published Naked Warriors (1919), Eclogues (1919) and the criticism that made him the leading English art critic of the 1930s. He was a founder of the Institute of Contemporary Arts and a lifelong anarchist, and died at Stonegrave, Yorkshire, on 12 June 1968.

literary_identity: Poet; the finest English poet of the First World War to be killed in it, and the most clear-sighted of the war poets.
biography: Born Charles Hamilton Sorley in Aberdeen on 19 May 1895; he was educated at Marlborough and went up to University College, Oxford, in 1913, but enlisted in the Suffolk Regiment in 1914. He was killed by a sniper at Hulluch on 13 October 1915, and his Marlborough and Other Poems appeared in 1916.

biography: Born Robert Malise Bowyer Nichols on the Isle of Wight on 6 September 1893; he served in the Royal Field Artillery on the Western Front, was invalided out with shell shock, and published Invocation (1915) and Ardours and Endurances (1917), which made him famous as a war poet. He taught at Tokyo and wrote plays and broadcasts, and died at Cambridge on 17 December 1944.

literary_identity: Poet and art historian; the author of 'For the Fallen', the most famous poem of the First World War.
biography: Born Robert Laurence Binyon at Lancaster on 10 August 1869; he worked in the Printed Books department of the British Museum and became Keeper of Oriental Prints and Drawings, publishing the poetry of Lyric Poems (1894), Odes (1901) and The Winnowing Fan (1914). 'For the Fallen' appeared in The Times on 21 September 1914. He died at Dunedin, New Zealand, on 10 March 1943.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Canadian; the war elegy and the front-line doctor
literary_identity: Physician, soldier and poet; the author of 'In Flanders Fields', the most widely read poem of the First World War.
biography: Born John McCrae in Guelph, Ontario, on 30 November 1872; he studied medicine at Toronto and McGill, served in the Boer War, and in 1914 went to France as a gunner and then as a medical officer with the Canadian Field Artillery. He wrote 'In Flanders Fields' after the death of a friend at Ypres in 1915, was promoted to lieutenant-colonel, and died of pneumonia at Wimereux on 28 January 1918.
literary_profile: John McCrae wrote 'In Flanders Fields', the most widely read poem of the First World War and the origin of the poppy as the symbol of remembrance: it was the single most influential piece of writing to come out of the war, reprinted across the world and used in every subsequent commemoration.
stylistic_characteristics: The rondeau with its refrain; the image of the poppy and the lark; the direct address from the dead; the plain, formal, public line; the appeal to the living.

biography: Born Charlotte Mary Mew in Bloomsbury on 15 November 1869; her family was visited by mental illness and two of her siblings were committed, and she and her sister Anne lived in poverty, making artificial flowers to support themselves. The Farmer's Bride (1916), The Rambling Sailor (1929) and her stories followed. She died in a nursing home in London on 24 March 1928.

literary_identity: Poet; one of the most original English woman poets of the period and a pioneer of the poetry of female rebellion.
biography: Born Edith Alice Mary Harper in Wimbledon on 21 April 1883; she grew up in Australia, married the solicitor Patrick Hepburn in 1906, and published The Contemplative Quarry (1915) and The Man with a Hammer (1916). She was a friend of D. H. Lawrence, was institutionalised more than once, and died in London on 30 April 1947.
